SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview of
Zilner T. Randolph
Tapes One and Two

Chicago, Illinois
February 13, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
MR. DE MICHAEL: Interview with Zilner T. Randolph, Part One, conducted by Don DeMichael at Mr. Randolph's home, Sangamon 6557 South Sanglin Street, Chicago, February 13th, 1977.
-- Of course, now, you have -- you know the date because they have it. I was born on January 28th, 1899, in Durham, Arkansas. I think you have that.
Yes. And Zilner -- was that common name then, or is that a family name?
Zilner -- a German named me.
Really?

Yes. See, my mother was a seamstress. She was a professional seamstress and something happened to her machine and she had to send for this technician to come and fix it. And at the time he came she told me -- she was still pregnant with me -- so she said the German told her, he says, 'Now, that, if the baby be a boy, name him Zilner, and spell it z-i-l-n-e-r.' And so she wrote that down and so she named me Zilner.
[PAUSE]
I'll be darned. You were mentioning earlier that you and your brother were getting into music. About how old were you when you started playing guitar?
Around about ten years old.
Uh-huh.
This was around about 1909 and I'm
always a year ahead of the year, see, in 1909 I'm ten, see. So I was about ten years old at that time.
Was it just a guitar around the house or was there a neighbor who played guitar?

It was a guitar around the house, but it was a friend of ours. His name was Lawrence. All I can remember is Lawrence, name -- I don't know his last name. But Lawrence and the first ting he taught me to play was Jim Canen, and also after he taught us the Jim Canen then he played the blues and we learned how to play the blues. And I still play those old blues yet. Blues that I played way back there when I was a boy around about nine or ten years old.
What were some of their names?
Well, all I know, Jim Canen. I don't know. Would you like to hear that Jim Canen?
Yes. uh-huh. Oh, you still play guitar.

Yes, uh-huh. I don't do too much of it now because -- just enough. Now, the Jim Canen was nothing but just -- we played finger style, which at time we called it the finger style, but it's the classic as I know, the classic, and it -- cause when you play with the pick (unintelligible) when you play with the fingers, it's pizicato, see.
Yes.
But I didn't know that at that time.
I didn't know pizzicato from (unintelligible) Now, here's the other thing
[Jim Canen]
(music)
Were you doing that ending when you were ten years old? That's a little modern touch that you added.

Well, unfortunately, I didn't know anything about that ending that I just did, because that ending entailed a C6, well, I didn't know anything about a C6. I just did it just to play an ending. Now, with the blues, whenever I would go in and all the men would be playing blues, they'd get up and say, 'Give Randolph the guitar,' see, because I'd have the blues and here I'd go.
(music)
Bet you didn't use that chord in 1909 either.
No, I didn't use that chord.
That was a pretty chord.
No, I didn't use that chord either, not that one.
That [Jim Canen] sounds like sort of a reel -- a folk dance number.
Well, I guess so. You know, the years takes a toll and, you know, I used to really could play that, being young and the dextrose of my fingers was really active
and I could play it very, very fast, but this time I haven't got that speed now.
Sure, I understand.
I'm 78 now, you know, different from a boy's fingers, ten year old kid's fingers and (then) a 78 --
Yeah.
Yeah, yes.
Well, did you play at dances, picnics and things like that?

We played for -- they call -- back there in those days they would have what you call a beer drinking parties and when they had the beer drinking parties, funny thing, they wouldn't exclude -- they wouldn't -- kids wasn't allowed. We didn't fool with beer -- we didn't drink the beer, we just go for the music, and everyone know that the Randolph kids played the guitar, so they'd ask me and my brother. So we would play -- practically be the music part.
I see.
Yes.
Did you get any pay for that or was it just for fun?

Fun. Me and my brother -- just fun. We'd go in there and it'd tickle us. You know, we was just glad to get to play. And now, it's a funny thing. I don't know if you've heard about this dancing or not. They call it
buck dancing.
Yes.
Yes. Buck dancing and what you would have to play --
(music)

That chord -- let me see. And he's cutting all kind of -- and sometimes while this is going on he's talking. And he's really talking and dancing all at the same time. That's what my brother would be doing when we put on these shows. We'd put these shows on and when one would sing we would have to play the accompaniment, play the accompaniment and each -- well, sometimes we would have duets together and I would have to sing the second part and he would sing the lead.
Did he play guitar also?
My brother?
I mean, would you play guitar duets?
No, we didn't play --
You would play guitar and he would sing and then sometimes both of you would sing.
And then sometimes he'd take the guitar and then we'd sing.
I see.
Of course, we only had one guitar.
Were there a lot of -- this was in a rural part of Arkansas, wasn't it?

Yes. This was in a little small town. One place called Chico, Arkansas, that we stayed in. All over Arkansas in a way of speaking. Then we stayed in a place called Jennings, Arkansas, and that's where we put on our shows, in Jennings, Arkansas. We put those shows on and people would come to them. Now, our audience was integrated at times.
Yes.
And --
This is other than the beer drinking parties? This is where you and your brother would charge admission to the shows?

Yes. Of course, we'd grown up and were a little older then. About 11 years old, 11 and 12. And I never will forget it, the year of the Titanic, that was 1912, you know, that's when the Titanic went down.
Yes.
That's when me and my brother got shipped off to Hot Springs to school to the parochial school.
Your mother sent you there?
Yeah, she sent us there. Then we -- Presbyterian school, and then we studied music.
Uh-huh.
And my brother, he stayed at school awhile, so when school was out he didn't come back to school and he didn't come home, so we wondered where was brother. I
wondered where he was. And I was a sick soul. So, here's what happened. He joined Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey's and then one --
Joined them as what -- a musician?

Yeah, he joined the show. And then when we come back -- and so he came back to school one day and everybody was ran to see -- they called him Jonas -- "Here come Jonas, Here's Jonas. Jonas is back." So, he asked Mrs. McBain -- she was assistant principal.
What was her name?

Mrs. McBain, and her husband, Dr. McBain, a doctor of divinity, he was the principal and she was assistant -- man and wife team there at the school. He asked her to let the kids come out to see him at the show. So, they was glad to see Jonas and so she didn't have any school one day. She just let -- that was a free day.
Everybody could go to the circus?
Everybody went to the circus to see Joe. Now --
What was he doing with the circus?
Yeah, now -- he and Mantan had an act --

Moreland
Mantan Mollen --
Yes.
You ever heard of Mantan --
Sure, I saw him many times.
Yes, uh-huh. Well, Mantan and my brother had an act. They was in the side show. And they sang and danced and he's they're still dancing and singing, dancing and singing.
I'll be darned. When was this about?

This was in 1912, 1913, 1914, round about 1914, I believe. Somewhere around (skew) 1914. And while Mantan was up doing his dance my brother -- I was out in the audience andhe saw me, and he held five fingers up there and he took and thumped a nickel out [there]. Yes, we had a wonderful time that evening. I stayed there almost until dark. Yeah.
Well, at school you say you started studying music formally.
Yes. I studied the piano.
Piano.
I studied piano.
Was this the traditional way of studying piano -- scales and pieces?
I used the same book now that she taught me out of. Matthews Standard Graded Courses for the Piano Forte.
I see. Did you get any harmony and theory at that time?
Not that year -- I mean, not when I was at this school at this time. But later on, later on I did. I studied harmony and theory. And I'll get into that if you want
me to.
Well, let's finish with the Presbyterian school first. You studied just piano? You hadn't started trumpet yet?

Uh-huh. No, I didn't have the trumpet. I studied piano. I'll tell you how the trumpet came in there after a while. And so, the principal would give -- the assistant principal. -- she would give recitals, you know, in the church, and I would play them. They'd give plays and that was quite an act. They say you shouldn't -- they say always stay away from the eyes I's, but the truth of the matter is I was really apt, so I played the part of the king and I wish you could have seen me sitting up there with a crown on and a red robe. A blood red robe and a crown, and I had to sing a song about if I was King Alcohol, many wonderful things I'd do. I'd make things flow and I'd have whiskey flowing down the avenue.
This is a church school?

Yes. And I played that role so -- I played that role so superbly, the girls -- and they were pretty girls too -- all the girls threw flowers at me and I didn't have sense enough to pick the flowers up. And when one of the teachers says to me, she said, "Zilner, why don't you get your flowers?" I didn't know you had to get the flowers. Well --
What kind of music did you play at the recitals? Ragtime was very strong in the St. Louis area,
which of course is not too far from Arkansas.
Well, no. She was strict, you would have to play just that --
(music)
Music like that kind.
Little pieces.
Uh-huh.
Had you ever heard of Blind Boone?
I didn't get a chance to hear him but I heard my mother talking about him. They say he was a wonderful pianist.
I heard some rolls that he cut around 1908, '10, something in there.
Piano roll, yeah.
Just a marvelous player, unbelievable. Like Tatum.
Yeah. Oh, yeah?
Just marvelous. He had a piece, the 2 gavotte, that he went through the whole cycle of fifths in like four bars.
Yeah?
In running.
In running.
Yes. It was unbelievable. I didn't know people played like that, and I thought maybe you had heard
him at that time.
Well, no, I didn't get a chance to hear him. But I'll tell you who I did hear, and it was James P. Johnson.
Oh. In Arkansas?
James P. Yes. Well, I didn't get a chance to see him, but I heard -- you know --
The piano roll.
Yeah, his piano rolls, because I used to sit and copy that.
Carolina Shout?
Yes. You know, he had a way of tenting, and I couldn't make those tenths. He'd make the tenths with one hand and he would go --
(music)
And while that tenths is going on this righthand is going --
(music)
And you would be surprised, (unintelligible) try to get that but, see, I couldn't make that. That was some stretch, because the best I could do would have to break it and it wouldn't sound --
It would roll.
-- yeah, and break that by rolling my hand. And it wouldn't sound as good.
Well, did the teachers frown on your listening to James P. Johnson and other rolls?

Well, no, they didn't. No, they didn't because I heard a teacher mention about some player -- somebody playing the piano and she said he was sit his fingers down and all his fingers would be playing the chords. But I had little pieces and things that I would play that had the girls around fanning me, you know, the girls would fan me while I'd be playing the pieces and, oh, my goodness. I thought was just in heaven, just rising, having those girls be fanning me and playing.
Is that the time that you decided that you were going to be a musician?
Well --
A full-time musician?

I decided that I was going to be a musician way back when I was fooling around with the guitar before I ever went to school. I was going to play because that fascinated me. That music was -- and I told my father to get me a guitar andhe said, "Huh-uh, no guitar." You know, he had a hang-up on that [point], that's a terminology musicians use a lot of times. It's because he said guitar players was pimps and rounders. Well, he was right in a way about some of those guitar players, because I remember how they were dressed. They had a Stetson hat and a blue serge trousers,
a starched and ironed jumper, starched -- white starched shirt and the collar standing open, and they'd have all of this gold --
On their teeth.

-- on their teeth, and they would have the guitar strung around and they'd have a gang of women behind them just like that. And they were playing and grinning but they're not tickled, you know why they're grinning --
Yes, to show the gold.
To show the gold.
Like Jelly Roll Morton with his diamond in his front tooth.
And that was the bag he didn't want me to get into.
Well, I can understand it.
I wouldn't have gotten into that bag. All I wanted -- if I -- I wished now, the way, if you've heard some of Joe Pass --
Yeah?
If you've heard some of Joe Pass, that --
I've known Joe for many years.

That man is something else. That man is something else. Now, I could have had a chance to study the guitar -- maybe I might well have been -- instead of a trumpet player, I might have been a celebrated guitarist. But, when I
left the school -- this was grammar school, as you know.
Yes.

And when I'd go home there wasn't any piano there, unfortunately, so I bought me a trumpet. And by knowing music I just bought me a trumpet and started studying a trumpet. All I had to do was get the fingering, because I know music on the piano, see. Because I used to sit and write music all the time, all right, so I started to playing the trumpet and I played the trumpet in the band.
Which band was this?
This was the [E Tyler] band around in Helena, Arkansas.
About when was this?
This was in -- this was during the time of World War I, because my brother -- he got shipped out to the Army pretty soon after this. Around in 1916, somewhere like that.
You were about 17.
I was about 17 year old boy.
Were you still in high school then?
Yes, I was getting ready to -- yes, I -- when did I go to college? I went to college at an early age -- 1917, 1918 -- I was 19 years old. I went to Biddle.
Went to Biddle --
Biddle University.
That was in North Carolina.
North Carolina, yes. That was in 1917.
1917. But when you were back home in Arkansas and you were playing with the town band, what kind of music were you playing? Just the standard march repertoire?
March repertoire and standard numbers like Over There, Over There, the Yanks are coming -- da, da, da.
The patriotic --
Yeah, all that stuff like that.
Had you heard jazz by this time?

Yes, I heard -- let's see, who did I hear? I heard the records -- Sweatman, I believe I heard him on clarinet. He was a great clarinetist I heard playing. At that time they called it ragtime. It was ragtime music. And then it went from ragtime to jazz, but some of them called it hoke. They called it hokum. Did you ever hear that name kicked around?
Oh, sure.

Hokum, yeah, they called it hokum, because I know when -- this white boy I know, he came to St. Louis and told me to teach him some hokum. And he's teach me some legit. Well, I didn't have to be taught legit because I played all this triple time solos, 'Honeysuckle Polka' and 'From the Shore of the Mighty Pacific' by Herbert Clark, and 'Old Folks at Home' in three variations, so I didn't need -- I
felt that I didn't need anything else, because, see I was pretty well up there on the trumpet.
Well, back home beforeyou went to college, did you try playing any ragtime on the trumpet, or any musicians around there who wanted to play ragtime?

No, there wasn't any. I had one fellow around there. He played, but he played piano and he was doing -- what was he doing? Da-da-da-da -- Benton Overstreet, I think. Did you know -- did you ever hear of Benton Overstreet? I think Overstreet wrote that.
I don't know.
"Chicago."
Yeah, but he was just playing popular songs -- this piano player?
Yeah, he was just playing popular songs on it. But he was adding a whole lot -- he'd done a lot of improvising.
Figurations, as the ragtime players would say.

Yes, he certainly was. A lot of ornaments and decorations and everything. And he was really making it sound good, because I know -- I spoke to a young lady and I said, "I don't like such and such a number," and she'd say, "Say, you haven't heard --," I've forgotten the fellow's name now. She said, anyway, I'll just say John. She said, "You haven't heard John play it." So, I finally got a chance to hear the wrote (or co-wrote) 'Dixie' by James Bland
John play it and it didn't sound like it did when --
So, he was doing some improvising or (unintelligible) some configurations in there.
Yeah, improvising.
Well, when you went to college, did you continue to study music?
yeah, I continued to study. I was in the band there, in the band there in Biddle. A fellow by the name of T. B. Jones had charge of the band. Yes.
And was this a concert band or a marching band, or --
Yeah, this was a marching band. He played marches. I was young and flowery -- you know how youngsters are.
Sure.
And I played, and he'd give the signal for to go -- (unintelligible) and I'd go ta-ta-ta-ta- -- and kept going and it made him sore. I don't blame him.
In other words, you would improvise a little something at the end or --
I was giving that repetition to -- we call it turn back --
Turn around.
To turn back or turn around, one of those things. And that threw the band and the band heard the

lead so strong and they went back and when they kept playing it, all right, then he just stood up and he played and he played I wanted to take down/ and (unintelligible) he made me play, so I didn't do that any more.
He was shooting you through the grease, as they say.
Yeah.
How big a band was this at Biddle?
At Biddle? Oh, as near as I can think it was around about 25 or 30 musicians in there.
A fair size band.
Pretty good size band. Pretty good size band it was.
When was this? About 1918, 1919?
Around -- well, I got in the band around 1918.
uh-huh.

And, this is where I got a chance to really hear some good music. Did you ever hear of Coleridge S. Taylor? This was a colored composer. He composed "Hiawatha's Wedding Feast" -- one of the prettiest things you want to hear. I (unintelligible) first time I'd ever heard anything like that and I really enjoyed that. Of course, that was on the first trumpet. I was playing that, but I would have paid them to let me sit in on that. That was really good. And we had violins in there.

A fellow by the name of David Taylor, he was the first violinist and I was first chair trumpeter on that ting. But it was so pretty, because it started -- da-da-da-da- -- and on and on and on. This fellow had a -- he had a tenor solo that he had to sing and oh, if that fellow didn't get some hands on that solo. was singing "swake, swake" He could sing it (unintelligible) from Coleridge Taylor's "Hiawatha's Wedding Feast." [PAUSE - APPROVED]
-- songs that you played at Biddle?
At Biddle?
This was at Biddle -- the 'Hiawatha's Wedding Song?

Yes. Well, I don't know. That's been so long ago. But this particular one stood out in my mind. Other than just whenever they would have the devotion exercise in the morning, see, because it was a Presbyterian school too -- Presbyterian school. Oh, by the way, it's Johnson C. Smith now.
Oh, the university is Johnson C. Smith. What --
Some rich Johnson C. Smith left so much money so they changed its name.
What town was it in, or is it in?
Charlotte, North Carolina.
Charlotte, North Carolina.
Yeah, Charlotte, North Carolina.
Did you get into town much? Were
there town musicians that you heard then?

Well, no. The only time we went -- like this time like this fellow like I tell you, T. B. JOnes, he would carry the band up and they had this movie was showing some big picture for the Hawaiian -- some Hawaiian picture. So he had the band come and sit out on the -- something like a porch like over the theater, and we would sit out there and we'd play "Isle of my Golden Dreams" and all Hawaiian numbers. Da-da-da-da
To go with the movie.
Yeah, to go -- we'd play numbers like that and so that was -- we got a kick out of that too, playing. "And did you ever hear Isle of my Golden Dreams?"
No.
Da-da-da-da- -- that was very beautiful number.
(music)
I've heard that. It's called Isle of my Golden Dreams?"
Yeah, "Isles of my Golden Dreams." Yes.
It's similar to "Girl of my Dreams," which also is chromatic --
Yes, yes. That was pretty. That's about the only thing I can remember. Well, I guess too, because we liked the music and we got a little money on the side.
For playing the theater. Yes.
For playing the theaters, yes.
Well, by this time had you started arranging, or started studying composition in any way?
No, I hadn't started studying arranging or composition, I was just playing the horn. But I was jazzing, because the boys called me -- nicknamethey called me Jazz Baby.
What do you mean, you were --
The kids around school, you know.
Then you'd heard -- besides the Sweetman Wilbur Spelman records, you'd heard some other records by this time? Let'ssee, what year are we talking about? '17?
We're talking in -- we're in the 1914, '15, '16, '17, like that, and I didn't get a chance to hear too many records, because unfortunately we didn't have a record player.
But you heard other musicians?
I heard a few musicians, yes.
You mentioned earlier that you were in St. Louis for a while. Was this after you were in Biddle?

Yes, this is after -- yeah, this is after Biddle. See, now, I played -- after I left Biddle University I played in Durham, North Carolina, for the summer. That's where I met mywife. I played there and then --
What kind of band was it?
It was -- this was a ragtime band --

I don't know whether it was ragtime or whether we were playing ragtime -- we was playing everything -- ragtime and jazz and everything else, because we were playing such numbers like "Rose of Washington Square" and "Isles of my Golden Dreams," that was popular. And "I'm Forever Blowing Bubbles." That's the kind of music those people like.
Were you playing --
Very few blues -- very few blues that people would ask you to play. You'd have to play one steps and real sweet ballad songs -- they were calling for that.
This is for dancing?

Yeah, this is for dancing. And they would come up and ask you, "Would you please play "Bubbles?" That's a waltz. They liked waltzing. Believe it or not -- da-da-da-da-da- And we'd play waltzes. And, well, the people really liked music because you really would get a kick out of playing good music, you know, different from the music -- well, it's still music, I guess, it's young folks music. I don't particularly care for that because I'm just one man, though.
What are you referring to?
The music of today.
Oh, today. Uh-huh.
Yeah, popular music of today. See, I'm just one man. That's the reason I say I don't like to knock music -- other people's music, but you have your likes and
your dislikes and that's why I say, I'm just one man, you know. Everybody has their likes and dislikes, but I can't stomach that. That don't have to be on there.
Well, when you were in Durham, how long were you playing in the band then?
In Durham? Well, I played the whole summer there at Page's Park.
What year was this?
This was in the year of 19 -- somewhere around the year -- when was this now -- 1919 I believe. 1917 -- that's when it was, 19 -- I believe it was, somewhere --
So, you were about 20 years old?
1917 -- I was around about 1919 -- I was about 20, yes, 1919 I was 20.
And you got married in Durham?
I got married in Durham. I got married during -- that's right, I got married in 1919.
So that dates it right there.
That dates -- that's right. I married in 1919.
And how long did you stay in Durham, just the summer?
Well, no. I stayed in Durham for a good little while, then we got -- I got with the show playing -- leading the band with a little show starring Pigmeat Markham.
COTTON CONTENT
Oh, yes.
Yes. Pigmeat Markham was the star of that show. I traveled around for a while and then --
Traveled around the south?
Yes, all around in the south. Then we came back to Durham -- the show came back to Durham and made up there in Durham to travel all around and came back. Then the show disbanded.
Uh-huh.

And I think I went from there to -- I went to -- oh, I carried my wife home to see my mother. I went to Arkansas to see my mother. And then, while I was down there, I got a letter from Sullivan to join him with a band in Danville, Virginia.
Who was Sullivan?
Sullivan was a little drummer. That's all I know. He played drums. And it was a small combination -- drums, piano, clarinet, trombone and trumpet. Five pieces.
Sort of like a New Orleans style band.
Yes, and we played dances then.
Was it a fake band, or did you have a library?
No, we didn't have a library, we just -- that's what we did, just faked it. We called it the Green
Book. We just looked out of the Green Book. You had a number, 'why don't you play so and so', we just started to play it. (unintelligible)
Yeah. Was it sort of like the New Orleans bands, you know, that we hear from records --
Yeah, something like --
-- with cornet on top and the trombone on --
-- yeah, more like a dixieland, if I can think back.
Well, by this time I guess the Original Dixieland Jazz Band records were out.
Yes.
They were out in 1917, so --
Yes, because this little clarinet fellow we had, he was running all -- he was playing kind of obbligato runs all through the music, you know, while we were playing.
Uh-huh. Like the dixieland bands do.
That's right.
Did you think of it as being jazz or ragtime or just music?
Well, I have to think of it as being more a dixieland -- more dixieland than jazz. Yes.
And this was in Danville, Virginia?
Beg pardon?
HEMLOCK ERASABLE COTTON CONTENT
This was in Danville, Virginia?

Yes, this was in Danville, Virginia. Because, then we played there for a while. See, we were playing -- this was something of a -- he called it a dance school and stir them they were just that thick, you couldn't stand with a stick --
Yeah, dime a dance --
-- and they paid off well until the last week. Then the last week --
Uh-huh, then you get stuck.
-- the man -- we didn't know we played that week and the band was gone.
Uh-huh.
So, I didn't know where the boys went. One of the boys went one way, so I got a job playing at the Hippodrome Theater there.
In Danville.
In Danville. So, I played at the Hippodrome Theater for a while.
As the leader or as a side man?
Well, no, a side man band.
Playing theater --

The leader was named Walter Morrow. He played piano, and it was three pieces -- drums, piano and trumpet. And we would play all those big shows that come in there. And you know, this Eddie Heywood that wrote this
"Canadian" -- what's the name --
"Canadian Sunset."
"Canadian Sunset?"
He had a father who was a piano too.
Well, that's what I'm speaking about.
Eddie Heywood Hayward, Senior.

I met -- fortunately, I met his father. Well, now, his father -- I used to play all his father's arrangements because the shows would come through there and they would have on there, arranged by Eddie Heywood Hayward 81 Theater. He played at the 81 Theater, in Atlanta.
Yes, he was from -- is that the TOBA Circuit?

Toby TOBA Circuit, that's right. T-O-B-A Circuit. That's right. T-O-B-A. We had -- I played Whitman Sisters, I played Sidney Easton and Stewart -- Easton and Stewart and [Denvois]. He had a big troupe -- all those was on that SHW Toby Times, Toby's Time, and they had a circuit that they would play. You're really familiar with that circuit?
I've read a lot about it.

Yes. So, we played that for a while. Let me tell you something funny about that theater. Because this entails a lesson that I learned and I -- you see, we would go in the winter and sometimes they'd have those cold days and

the manager of the theater, he'd say -- he'd tell the girls, "Turn the piano on." She'd turn on the electric piano, and they'd tell us, "All right, you all can go home, it's all right." See, we played -- when they didn't have shows, they played the silent pictures anyway, see, played music for silent pictures. All right. But we'd get paid (less (unintelligible)) see.
What was the pay then, do you recall?

Well, it was a very small pay, around about $25.00 -- $25.00 a week. But $25.00 a week at that time and $20.00 a week, and the regular salary was $9.00 a week because men was getting a dollar and a half a day. So, I was kind of half-way rich.
Yes.

But anyway, now, you watch this twist. The man would send us home three and four times, all right? So, finally after awhile the business began to pick up. I'd look back and when the business picked up, the people were coming in -- oh, I was sitting up thereplaying and I'd be so angry, I would almost want to burst.
Angry because --
Because the people were coming in. Then I couldn't get a chance to go home. See?
I see.
So, okay. So, finally, after awhile business began to fall down again, so the man began to send us

home. So, finally, the man says, "Well, as bad as I hate to do this," he says -- and he only had three -- drums, piano and trumpet, he says, "I just have to keep the drums and the piano. I'll have to lay you off -- lay off the trumpet. Randolph, I'll just have to lay you off. I don't know when I can hire you back because the business is just too dull." You know? After that I had pulling for the man. I have really been pulling for the crowd, for the man. Do you follow what I mean?
Yeah, yeah.
I learned my lesson. I really learned -- that taught me a lesson.
I can see that.
So, that's how I got with the medicine show.
Oh, when you left the Hippodrome you went with a medicine show.
I went with the medicine show and I played with the medicine show.
What did you do in the medicine -- what kind of music did you play in a medicine show? Was that like a carnival?

No. This was just a -- this man -- he would sell medicine and he'd have -- to my idea, I think he would have a lot of chicken entrails in a bottle, in alcohol or something like that, and he would tell them that

these are parasites that he got -- you take this medicine and we would get it out and one of those things and he was selling the medicine for a dollar a bottle. And then he would talk and talk and talk. His name was Dr. -- I've forgotten his name -- Dr. somebody. But, anyway, strike up the band. And we'd strike up the band and then he started to selling this medicine. Only going for a dollar a bottle. I don't think I have but a few left. And the people was crowded around this thing. And, you know, we would start to playing. We play real fast music -- ra-ta-ra-ta -- one of those things. And while we're playing, he's selling medicine. He -- his helper was opening those crates -- opening those cartons and he's running backwards and forwards and that (unintelligible) flying.
Rock Tail was
How big a band was it?
Holt.

The boy's cousin on drums, I picked up a clarinet band, Holt was on the trombone, I was on the trumpet -- not too many. Just that piano -- no, no piano -- drums, trumpet, trombone and clarinet. We played such things as 'Storm and Sunshine' and 'Chicago Tribune March', you know. We had those. Re-de-le- -- you know, you know how they go.
Yeah.

And we play those things and it's funny, this man would really -- he'd really sell that medicine. He'd have his hands full -- you wouldn't be able to do that now because the guys would be out there to stick him up, trying to --
For the money, huh?
Yeah, had his hands full of money. He'd bring that back and he'd run out there and be selling and get moremoney and bring it back and we're just playing and people are buying that medicine.
You just barnstormed through the south?
Yeah, we would go -- he would set up and we would play three to four weeks at one time in the same place.
Oh, really?
Uh-huh. The medicine show.
I see.

And now, here's -- we had -- what we would do -- we had a nice little show. We had comedians and an escape artist. We had a fellow -- we had some big men would come up and tie that fellow -- tie him and he would get loose, just like that. They would come up there to tie and when they tied him we would be playing -- while they tied him we was playing da-de-da-de -- and they would just tie him up, but when the people get through tying him up, then we would hit into something fast, you know, we'd hit into something fast and after a while he'd start shaking and chord, he'd step right out of them. The cord.
That's right. Da-da-da-da -- but he
told us how he did that. He'd expand -- he would expand his chest when they were tying him --
When they were tying him.
Yes, and while they was tying him he'd expand everything this way. They'd be tying and the way he stood -- then, when he relaxed and straightened up, well -- there's tricks to all trades.
Sure, sure.
So, we played awhile and then in Greensboro, North Carolina. Then we left Greensboro, North Carolina and went to Cincinnati, Ohio.
Uh-huh.
The medicine show did. And then I sent my wife back home to stay until we could get a place. Well, we stayed there for awhile and the medicine show broke up there.
Where was home? Arkansas or Durham?
Durham.
Durham.

I sent her back home in Durham. Well, the show broke up and after that we went to look in the paper and we saw J. L. Cronan's Carnival Show where they needed a band. So, Holt wired them -- the trombone player wired them, so we went there and we joined them in Burlington, North Carolina. And that's where we played for the -- see, this was a 42-car carnival and we played the minstrel part. And, of
course, every evening we would have to go out in the town and play to draw the crowd and (unintelligible) The man would spiel
Ballyhoo.

Yes. So, the man would -- he would give -- this was comical, because he would give this speech and as soon as he said this punch word, then I'm supposed to hit right in to it, see. Well, the man said it so funny, you can't play and laugh -- not a trumpet, see. He would say -- now, here's his line, "Now, ladies and gentlemen, if you come and see our little show, we have --," he would tell about the girls we had on the show, so many girls, and the comedians, "and we want you to come end enjoy yourself and then you knock on everyone's door and tell them about this show. (But) Ladies and Gentlemen," now, this is what would get me, "if you come and you don't like the show, please don't knock."
(laughter)

And when he said that -- as soon as he said, "please don't knock," I got to say ra-da-da-da- -- that was something. So, I left that show for a while. I stayed there for awhile and I left them and went to Durham -- back to Durham and played in a fellow by the name of Watkins -- he owned a theater there. And I went there and took over the leadership of the band there.
When was this, about?
This was in 19 -- round about 1921.
Uh-huh.

I took over that show there and I played there for awhile. Didn't last any too long. Then what I did, I went right back home after I left -- after I played -- I guess we stayed in that theater about three or four months. Then I went back home to --
To Arkansas.

To Arkansas, Helena, Arkansas. And I played in a drug store. Believe it or not -- piano, drums and trumpet -- we played in the back of the drug store. They were selling roast beef sandwiches and brown gravy and so forth and I'm telling you that place was just like that.
Crowded.

Crowded. Well, I told the man, I says, "I have a very fine guitarist I know of back in Durham, North Carolina. I'd like to add him in the band here." So, the man told me to send and get him. So, I sent and got him and his name was Joseph Patterson. You'll read about that though, in that book about Patterson. So, I had Patterson, and I sent for Patterson and that's where we played. (unintelligible) Then we were trying -- and there was another place -- that man was about to go out of business, so he sent and got Swayzee and the rest of those boys, called themselves the Syncopated Six. I think they had played with Mamie Smith's Jazz Hounds.
Swayzee
Swese, yes, I know that name.
Yes. Swayzee trumpeter, [popular band.] Pretty good trumpeter.
Now, what town was this?
This was in Helena -- Helena, Arkansas. So, we had banjo, trumpet, drums -- Floyd Campbell on drums --
I know that name.
Floyd Campbell, yes, he played --
Played around here, didn't he?
Yes, uh-huh. Floyd Campbell did, had a band here and played here for quite a while. Yeah. And Cranston Hamilton -- he's dead now, he died not too long ago.
What did he play?

He played piano. Oh, (unintelligible) and he really played but didn't read a lick. He didn't read nothing, just played. He played something, he really played. He played with Charlie Creath and everything. So, --
In St. Louis?
Beg pardon?
Charlie Creath in St. Louis?

In St. Louis. Um-hum. So, then we played there for awhile and I took a notion I wanted to go to St. Louis. So, I told Patterson, I said, "Well, Patterson, we're going to St. Louis." So, I got -- I said, "All right, you want to go? Come on." Yeah. So, I got Patterson to St. Louis and

left my wife at home, because I always leave her whenever I go somewhere where I don't know where I'm going, in a way of speaking. I would leave her at home, see, because I don't to carry my wife there -- I don't know what I'm going to run into, see. So, I got a place -- a nice place, and soon I ran into her. Then, after I stayed there for awhile, I met this boy named [ ] Long and he introduced me to Charlie Creath. And Charlie Creath in turn asked me, he said, "Are you working?" I said, "No." He said, "Well, here, you take this. Take this and go to this address. My sister -- her name is Margie [Sisson.]" She was married to manager of Zutty Singleton. I guess you've heard of Singleton.
Oh, certainly.
Yeah, uh-huh.
Marg, yeah.
Yeah, uh-huh.
I didn't know she was --
So, I went to Marg and gave her the note. So, Marg like the way I played. I don't know what I was doing -- I was just blowing. She like the way I played, so she kept me in the band there.
You say Marg was your sister?
Marge was Charlie Creath's sister.
Yeah, and Zutty played around come up from New Orleans. St. Louis for awhile; (unintelligible)
Yeah, Zutty played, certainly did. That's where I met Zutty from, from St. Louis.
When was this, about '23, something like that?
Yeah. He's passed now.
Yes, he passed about a year -- a little over a year ago -- about a year and a half ago.
Uh-huh, yes.
Face. (unintelligible)
Yes, he certainly did. That boy really played some drums, though.
Yes.

Singleton, he was something! Well, then I played around and giged around there for awhile and then after I ran into this fellow -- dead now, Shirley Clay, he asked me if I wanted his permanent job. I told him yes. He said, 'Well, I'm going to New York,' he says, 'and you can have this job playing the theater,' -- the Cranshaw -- at the Hip -- no, at the Criterion Theater, just playing pictures, you know. Of course, you had toplay good music.
When silent movies came along, you know, came into town, did sheet music accompany them, you know, did you have certain music that you had to use?
Yeah, that's right, you had a score -- they would send you a cue sheet and you'd have to go buy or go

to the library. And at that time Sam Fox -- Sam Fox Folios -- you would have -- they had that music to offer -- you know, they know all about that I guess -- what kind of music to have in a library for pictures. And you could get that -- you get the number that they wanted or a facsimile thereof, you know.
Uh-huh.
And you'd get a chance to play -- well, we had to play all of the standard overtures and selections and things like that.
All these jobs were reading jobs in theaters, of course. (unintelligible)

Oh, yes, they were reading -- and you would get -- that's where you really get a kick because you play some pretty music. I never will forget the number where we would have Oriental pictures like something like the Japanese or something like that -- we would play "Japanese Sunset," and that was really pretty, really something. Come out of the (unintelligible) Sam Fox Folios, see.
Well, when you're in St. Louis, did you ever go to the Chauffeur's Club?
Yes, uh-huh.
That was a famous place down by the river, I think.
Yes, that's what I'm coming to. So, I stayed at the theater there for awhile and then I began to

practice on my horn and I got that foursome, you know, because I didn't have anything to do but just go to the theater, get off early, get up in the morning, practice on my horn and sit around, and I told my wife, I said, "I'm going to find me a teacher and go study." They called it thorough bass and harmony back there in those days. PAUSE I studied with Eddie Hudson. So, (stayed with) I studied with Eddie for around about four -- from 1922 until '25.
You were in St. Louis.
Yeah, well, after that, just a little longer than that. I left around about '26.
Did you know Frank Trombquer? Did you know any of the white musicians in St. Louis?
No. No, I don't know -- I got a chance to hear some of his -- Frank Trombquer's and some of Bix Beider-becke's tunes that they were doing -- things like that.
Uh-huh. They worked at the Arcadia Ballroom there.
Arcadia Ballroom, yeah. That's right, I heard about that.
I ran into a man who did some of the arranging for that band, Bud Hassler.
Oh, yes.
Well, go ahead with your story.
Yes. So, well, I studied there with

Eddie for about four years. I took harmony, theory of harmony then, Goodrich Analysis of Music -- now, there's where you learn something about music. Then -- and I passed -- I used that with my pupils too. A lot of the information I got out of the books with Eddie Hudson, such things like -- now, you know, we use bars out of context when we say bars. There's a bar line and there's a perpendicular line, see. See, (unintelligible) line runs horizontal and this perpendicular line is the bar line.

Now, that bar line divides the staff in two measures. They rewrite the notes in the measure and if some singer or dancer or even some orchestra leader comes up and they want you to play the last two measures, they'll tell you to play the last two bars. Well, the last two bars maybe sometime on a number is the last two double bars -- the last two bars which isn't anything, and I showed them that, about the last two bars. And such things like, pick up the time. You can't pick --
Pick up the tempo.

Yes, you can't -- that's right. You can't pick up that time, you see. And it's things like that I pass on to those -- pass on to them. And quite a few of the little pointers that I got out of Goodrich Analysis of Music, you know, where he takes the music and tears it all to pieces and analyses it. Well, finally, what I want to tell you about Hudson, after this fourth year, I went with Hudson to get my lesson there, and Hudson says to me, he says, 'Well,' he always

called me boy. He said, "Well, boy, four years ago when you came here," he says, "I said to myself, 'This funny looking little juggaboo --'," thats what we usually call one another sometimes, juggaboo, he says, "This funny looking little juggaboo say he's going to do like all the rest of the juggaboos, he's going to take one or two lessons and cut out.'"

He says, "But you didn't -- you kept coming." He says, "I have scratched my head many a day to dig up material for you," that's the average person would say what he said. Well, now (unintelligible) oh, yeah, I'm happy. One of these things, (unintelligible) but when he said that it was ______. A big lump hit me like in the stomach. I looked around in the room and I looked, and it was kind of -- I felt sad because I said to myself, "Now, you won't be coming back here any more."

I always looked forward to coming to Eddie, because Eddie always would sit after a lesson and he would talk me all night about staying out of pool rooms. I'm a married man now, but I'm a young man, see. And tell me, don't allow yourself to get used to something that you can't do without. Such things like that. He told me about a man fished around in an ash tray looking for a cigarette and had to get up at 3:00 o'clock in the morning and got in his car going around to this place to open so he could get a cigarette. He said -- without any -- I don't mean any offense, but he -- just speaking of Eddie Hudson telling me, you know. And so, he was telling me, "Don't allow yourself to get used to something that you just got to have, you just got
to have it." Well, that instilled in me, and I'm that way now, today. He really did wash my brain good.
That's a good philosophy.
Yeah. He give me a good brain washing.
And, so, it was sad for me to part from Eddie that way. Well, I went to Kreuger Conservatory for awhile, but I didn't stay therelong because the fact that I got this job playing with the roof garden.
This was in Milwaukee?
Yeah, Milwaukee.
Well, before you leave St. Louis, you were going to mention something about the Chauffeur's Club.

Oh, well, now. Now, here's the way this happened, the show at the Club. My (unintelligible) gave me the job, because he's going to Chauffeur's Club. Shirley Clay was going to Chauffeur's Club, so he had me to take the job at the theater. All right. So, finally, after I stayed there for awhile, Shirley came to me again and asked me if I wanted a job, if I wanted to come to Chauffeur's. He was going to New York.
Yeah.

I told him yes. I wanted it -- and I really wanted it because the leader and I wasn't getting along any too well, and this way -- they tried to put this in the paper, like I said it I say, but he missed -- now, I laughed about the piano -- and the

leader at the theater was kind of jealous in a way. He didn't have a piano and when I bought my piano then it made him jealous. Then he wanted me to buy a horn. Well, now, he knew that the theater was paying -- that theater there was paying $25.00. Now, he knew $25.00 a week and paying for a piano and paying for room, paying for my room rent, or whatever it was, me and my wife, where was staying, and to have to , you know, pay upkeep of the wife and things like that -- why, he figured that something got to give.
You couldn't afford a new horn.

Couldn't afford a new horn. But, yeah, see. So, when he told me I had to have a new horn, see, the boss was kicking on me. I went to the boss -- I'm thinking that the boss is kicking, I said -- and I switched it around turned the thing around when I went to the boss, see. I said, "Louie, I want to see you just a minute." Louie came to me and said, "Yes, what do you want?" I said, "My horn is playing me kind of bad and," I says, "what I'd like to do," I said, "I'd like for you to buy me a new horn and take it out -- take out a few dollars each week until I pay for it." He says, "Your horn playing you bad?" He says, "I don't see nothing about your horn playing bad. It sounds all right to me." I said, "Do you like the way it sounds?" He said, "Yes, I like the way it sounds." He say, "Yeah, I said, "Okay, all right (Unintelligible)" "Save the money," he told me, "Save the money." I said, "Okay." So, then I knew
what it was all about.
He was jealous of you.
Yeah.
You were playing cornet?
Yeah, well, I played a trumpet.
You were playing a trumpet back then?
Yeah, I had the trumpet then. But I didn't let on one thing. I didn't go back and tell the leader one thing, you see.
What was the leader's name?
[Cranshaw].
[Cranshaw]

[Cranshaw] I heard he was passed on now. So, then, when Shirley Clay came and told me he was going to New York and asked me would I take this job, why, then, you know I wanted to get away from [Cranshaw]. I told him yes. Then the job was paying $10.00 more. See, I was getting $25.00 at the theater and there I was getting $35.00 at Chauffer's Club. So, I went to Chauffer's Club.
What kind of band was that? Was that more of a jazz band and blues?
Yeah -- dixieland. We played strictly dixieland, because Powell was the leader then. James Powell was the leader and he played clarinet. And we really had a dixieland band.
Who else was in the band, do you recall?

Yeah. Isaac Jefferson, piano; Pat Powell, leader on clarinet; Dial Dyre was on drums; and, well, we had Lightfoot George Life at one time on saxophone, when Life left we had a boy by the name of [Swain] on the saxophone. And I was on the trumpet.
uh-huh. And what kind of tunes did you plan then? Did you play some blues by then?
Well, we played all kinds -- we played blues, we played 'Snag It' -- that's one of Louie's and Joe Oliver's numbers.
Yes. Did you play the break -- da-da-da-da-da-da-
Yes, but I played that when Pat Powell would get mad -- that was a tune he'd stomp off to punish you. He'd stomp 'Snag It' off this way -- one, two, three, four --
Really?
But you see, that didn't bother me -- that was triple tongue time you see -- di-di-di-di -- That's the way I played that you see, and that got him. I played triple tongue time, so --
Was Singleton Palmer around in those days?
Who's that?
Singleton Palmer -- tuba player. He might have come a little later.
He might have come a little later. I'll tell you who I met, though --
Ben Thigpen?
Yeah, Thigpen was around in those days. Now, this Thigpen that I hear of -- so much talk of, that must be his son.
That's his son, yes.
I told my wife that was his son.
Were some of the St. Louis men playing on river boats at that time?
Yeah.
Charlie Creath was --
Yeah, Charlie, yeah.
-- well known.

We had a fellow on piano by the name of Burroughs Lovingood. Yeah. Burroughs Lovingood. We sent and got Lovingood from there. Well, I can tell you about that a little later on. So, I played there for awhile. It's a funny thing, though, while I was there, while I was studying, when I was at the Chauffeur's Club. Boy, they had some beautiful waitresses -- very beautiful girls, and they couldn't understand why all the boys would be up there buying those club sandwiches and setting the waitresses up and why is it Randolph don't come up here?

What's the matter that you all hate the trumpet player? Why does he -- why is it that he didn't come up here? They say, "Well, he's sitting back out there building air castles." That's what they were saying. I was studying at this time. This was before Hudson had told me that -- I had -- he had given me all he could -- had exhausted his vocabulary or what have you. So, I played fair and went on and on until a fellow by the name of Chauffeur Inge came to Chauffeur's Club and I wondered why he kept a hanging around and listening and looking, and I noticed he looked at me and he kept looking at me and listening. Every time I'd go to play, he'd -- I wondered, I said, "I wonder what gives with the fellow?" But he wouldn't -- he didn't say anything to me. So, finally, on the last time, this guy asked me if I'd like to -- if I'd take a job on the Roof Garden. And I told him, I said, "Oh, yes, I'll take the job, sure. I'll take the job on the Roof Garden." So, finally, one time -- one Sunday night he called me up and said, "This is Eddie Inge." He says, "I'm calling from Milwaukee." He says, "Do you want this job?" I says, "Yes." He says, "Well, I told the man about you and he says if you come up here you can get this job." I said, "Tell him you know what I'm going to tell him now. (unintelligible). Tell him to send me a ticket." So, he sent me the ticket. And then I put my notice in and I went to Milwaukee.
When you were in St. Louis, did you hear any of the New Orleans bands on the boats?
Unfortunately I didn't get a chance to get to the boats. No. Because playing at the theater I was playing every night, didn't have a night off. Then when I was at the Club I didn't have a night off.
Had you heard any of the records -- by this time the Oliver Creole Jazz Band records were out. You had mentioned Snag -- How did you learn Snag?

Yes, I heard Louie -- I had heard Louie and Oliver -- I had heard Louie's record and after hearing Louie, oh, I made arrangements of a lot of Louie's stuff. I made arrangements on Snag for the band that we played with. I made arrangements on that.
Yeah, but that was Oliver's tune. What did you hear of Louie -- did you hear the Louie Hot Fives by this time?

Yes. I heard Louie Hot Five, I heard "Cornet Chop Suey," and I used to play the "Cornet Chop Suey" and the "Oriental Strut" -- I used to play that, that "Oriental Strut" was pretty too. And the Strut was (unintelligible). Yes, all those Louie tunes.
Yeah.
Yes, and --
Were you patterning your playing on Louie at this time?
I think I just leaned toward Louie then
after hearing Louie -- I'll tell you what I heard. I heard Louie and Bessie Smith once. Someone played the organ --
yes, the St. Louis Blues -- Fred Longshaw.
Yes, someone had played --
Played that little organ.
-- played a little organ and Louie was playing the trumpet and Bessie Smith was singing, and I never heard such thing --
A very moving record. The St. Louis Blues, the three of them doing that.
And Louie was playing -- Louie was really playing some pretty horn.
Uh-huh.

So, I said, 'That's the kind of horn I want to play, I want to play that.' That's a funny thing about my playing and my hearing of tunes. Whenever I hear a tune, I hear it in two veins. I hear in Louie vein and a Coleman Hawkins vein. And I can duplicate either one for you on the paper.
Uh-huh. Louie's very lyrical, Hawk is very vertical (very vocal) -- harmonic player.
Yes, that's right.
Interesting.
Now you take Hawkins -- and I have some

of my pupils sometimes doing the same thing. And I try to hum it to give them the idiom, you know. That idiom that Hawkins for instance, if Hawkins, does with that -- (unintelligible) if he's going to pay a number like -- let's just say "Don't Blame Me" (unintelligible) like dum-dum-da-da- -- Hawkins would say -- do-do-do-do- Well, I write that kind of thing. See, and I try to give it to them. And the trumpet's the same way. But sometimes you can -- well, it's like that old mule I used to plow when I was a boy. I used to think because I was really thirsty, the mule was thirsty and I would try to make him drink. I couldn't make him drink.
Lead a horse to water, right.
Well, you took the job in Milwaukee and that was the -- what was -- the Wisconsin --
Wisconsin Roof Garden. Two bands.
Was that a ballroom?
Ballroom. And what a ballroom. They had a place called Peacock's Alley and that's -- that was one of the prettiest places you want to see in your life.
Was this downtown?
Yeah, on Wisconsin Avenue, right downtown. Atop of the Wisconsin Theater.
I see. Then, the clientele was white?
All white, yes, all white.
And were both bands black?
No, no, white and colored band.
I see. Now, Ed Inge --
Well, it's a funny thing. We weren't supposed to be just a black band. We were supposed to be Creoles.
Oh, I see.
(unintelligible).
Who had the band?
Bernie Young had the band.
And Ed Inge --
Inge was an arranger and I was an arranger.
I see. By this time you were writing arrangements?

Oh, yes, I was arranging then. I was using (unintelligible) characteristic of chords and rhythms that they are really doing (now) I was doing it back then in those times. Because everybody will tell me, you were ahead, and they couldn't -- and I had a hard time getting it through -- getting my work over, because of a little ahead of he had a time and they couldn't understand it.
In what way do you mean -- rhythmically?
Rhythmically was one way. The chords the characteristic of chords, they like the way it sound but they couldn't understand it. Then I wrote more like -- counter-

point. For instance, you're playing, but you -- you're playing with me in the section, but maybe you wouldn't be playing just the same thng that the other fellow's playing, you see. I wrote more in a counterpoint way.
Yes, voices.

Voicing, that's right. See, most of the bands wrote more concerted, you know, concerted way -- concerted like -- da-da-da-da -- well, if I would say da-da-da- see, I've got them mixed up in there. Then, I would have maybe the saxophones trilling -- this is very beautiful. The saxophone would be trilling on a certain chord -- while they're trilling on a certain chord, then I pick a tone out for their chord that's very brilliant and put the trumpets on there and let them give you somewhat of an offbeat. da-da-da-da Then I throw the rhythm against that ba -ba-ba-ba -- Then I would let my trombones come up ba-ba-ba-ba -- and all that mix. Well, when the trumpets get so high, then I would let them hit together and spread -- da-da-da-da-da--
Uh-huh, yeah.
I had a lot of fun.
Well, did you write for Bernie Young's band?
Oh, yes. Yes, I wrote for Bernie Young's band.
Well, how big a band was that? I've

I never will forget Louie -- we just got into a place in Washington, Washington, D.C., and Joe Glaser says, 'We're going to broadcast,' and I said, 'Louie just got in he's got his cot down, and he's and (unintelligible) going to sleep.' He said, 'Well, he'll have to get up because we're going to broad --' I said, 'No, Louie got to have his rest. The man has got to have his rest. The man is tired. Louie is not going to broadcast.' That made Joe mad and made his wife mad -- not Lucille now, this was Alpha -- this was the other girl.
Oh.
She got mad -- Alpha got mad because I was telling Louie what to do. But, see, I was looking out for the man's health. And we was -- those one-nighters was
Yeah.
We was playing those one-nighters, wasn't getting a chance to sleep. So, I didn't wake him up, told them don't bother Louie, (unintelligible) let him sleep.

You were talking about the Sunset All Stars. And you said that Jabbo Smith was in there, and Zinky Zooty Singleton. Was Preston Jackson in the band?

This was in 19 -- I believe it was, yes. But this is before Louis came back from --
Yes.

France. And so, Cal Dickerson said, "Well, that's all now. Let's Just go." Then Joe says, "Well, what about that man over there?" Well, see, Cal Dickerson didn't have -- he really didn't want me. He didn't want me in the band, but I was just in there because Joe had an angle. See, Joe was giving me a job, because he's going to have me to
organize the band for Louis. And I didn't know Louis was telling Joe this, you see.
Oh, I see.

I didn't know this was going on. So Al Dickerson says -- he leaned over on the piano, he says, like this, "What are you going to play, man?" And so, I obliged him. I was full of accommodations that day, and I said, "The Peanut Vendor", man."
(Laughter.)
So, I played The Peanut Vendor. So knowing that Joe liked Louis on the trumpet, and sang it like Louis.
Oh, yeah?
And Joe got a kick out of that.

Yeah, I knew Leon.
Scottie, yes. Nice little trumpet player.

Well, I don't know. You know, some-

times they had those little hidden things going on, and maybe you don't know -- I don't know about it, you know. Maybe the journalists or something like that and the media might know something. But as far as some of the musicians, they keep some of those things here, because here's the way this turned out.

Oh, well, this is --
This is in 1933.

Well, no. I got the band --no, this band I got together after the -- after I left the show.
I see. The --
After the show. See, I toured with Pass and Review, 1933, with Joe Glaser -- see, Joe Glaser -- and you remember Leo Salkins, the booker downtown?
Uh-huh.
Well, Leo Salkins had the -- he had this show. And in time we had Billy and Millie, was the only
two colored on there. They had about 62 white -- 60 white, I think. About 60.
In the show.
In the show.

Yeah, Mezzrow and Joe Glaser.

This -- yeah, sometimes I get those years mixed up.
Let's see. The Century of Progress was in 1933, I believe, wasn't it? The exposition?
'33, '34. This must be '33. Yes, I believe this was '33, when I organized the band.

Canetti
Yeah, that was --

[Cossetti], the booker?
Yeah, he was the booker over in France or something like that.
Oh.

From France, yes.
In the '35 band that you put together for him.
Yes, yes, but -- well, I would say '34, I believe.
'34 he put the band --
Uh-huh. '34, because we were with this outfit during '33 and when it was over with Louis came back, and I got the band together for Louis.
Okay. Could we go back a few years and talk about the 1931 band for a little while? The first band.
The very first band.
Yes.
All right.
The one with Tubby Hall and --
Tubby Hall and Lester Jackson.
Yes.
And Charlie Alexander, Al Washington,
George James, Lester Boone and --
Mike McKendrick.
Mike McKendrick.
Right. We talked a bit about that the other time.
Uh-huh.
