I joined it at the Greystone, yeah.
And there's been a lot written about when the band went back to -- or, when Louis went back to New Orleans --
New Orleans, yes. I was with him at that time, when he went back.
Do you recall the reception? There's supposed to have been a great reception for Louis and --
It was. They had -- it was very good, and the last I remember seeing Louis, the crowd picked him up, and Louis was kicking -- that was comical.
Was this a black crowd, a white crowd?
Well, these was all blacks.
Uh-huh.
All blacks, that picked him up. And I said, 'Well, we don't know where to go.' And so he said something about, go to Patterson's Hotel. Said, 'Louis, go to

Patterson's Hotel." So we went to Patterson Hotel, and finally -- that's where we found Louis, Patterson's Hotel, there on -- oh, I haven't been in New Orleans in a time. Patterson's Hotel on -- I forgot the name of the street now. Antoine or something. No, that's Detroit.
Well, anyway, did they have bands playing, some of the musicians that were down there when Louis was younger? Were they there?
I tell you who got together, I got a band -- organized a band, and someone said, there's a band down here now. See, we went to stay four weeks. I think we stayed four months. And this --
This is at Suburban Gardens.
Yeah, Suburban Gardens. And they said, this band sounds just like Louis, and whenever he sings, he says, oh, you dog and everything. And Louis was singing, and come to find out it was Louis Prima.
Louis Prima, sure, yeah. Copied everything that Louis did.
Yeah, Louis Prima.
Well, the Suburban Garden; was that a ballroom or a nightclub or what?
It was a ballroom, a dinner -- what do you call it -- supper club.
Uh-huh.
And a gambling place.
Did they have shows, or was it just a band featured?
Excuse me. Just the band featured.
Well, you must have did very good business.
Oh, did it.
To stay there four months.
Did it. Tell you what, there was a fellow came out there, says, 'Louis, play Shine'. I just lost $10,000.'
This was a white club.
This was -- yeah, white place.
But Louis was quite popular with the white people and --
Oh, yes, very much so. Very much popular.

There's also a story about the opening night at the Suburban Gardens and a broadcast that was to take place, and the announcer wouldn't announce Louis. Is that true, that he wouldn't announce Louis because Louis was black and he was a white announcer?
Well, no. Here's what they got mixed up. They got this mixed up about when -- of course, all the announcers, they announced him in a broadcast, but they had a

baseball team called the Pelicans. And they made Louis an honorary member of the Pelicans. So Louis was telling about the game and telling them to come out there. This was -- excuse me for laughing -- this was down in New Orleans, and Louis said, "We're going to take them like Grant took Richmond."
(Laughter.)
Wrong thing to say.
Wrong thing to say. Brother, did the letters pour in.
Oh, he said it over the air?
Yes, that was over the air. Louis didn't know.
(Laughter.)
So they told Louis, "Don't say that. Don't say that no more."

Well, did Louis do any jamming when he was down there, that you know of? Earl Hines told me that when they were playing together in Chicago with the Sunset, I guess this was in '27, '28, that Louis always kept his mouthpiece in his pocket, and he and Earl would go out after they got through and sit in every place.
Did Louis continue that on the road?
No, he didn't do any of that, no. No, because Louis worked so devilish hard, when he got through, he'd go and hit the sack.
Uh-huh.
Yeah, he'd hit the sack. No, he didn't do that.
Did you ever do any small band things, you know, on gigs like just trumpet, clarinet and trombone and a rhythm section, do any of the old tunes, or fake some things?

No. He would always do the band. I'll tell you one thing that I saw down there. They had a little program, a little show -- this was in the theatre, because this was entertaining the blacks. And I saw Louis and this -- I'll say his first wife, I guess, Lil -- I guess you know Lil.
Oh, yes.

Uh-huh. Well, Louis and Lil put on an act, honest to goodness, I had never seen such a superb act. That act was immaculate. Those two people performed. I didn't know -- they looked like they could just breathe together. They knew what one another was doing, and I said to myself, "It's a shame that she's not in some kind of a show."

Well, they said she was a good dancer. But she didn't do too much dancing, but just the witty little things that she and Louis would do. And she would sing, Louis would play the horn. Then, they would start ribbing one another and kidding one another on the show. And their act was -- the band enjoyed it more so than the people did.
Well, Lil was in New Orleans with Louis?
With Louis, yeah. She was in New Orleans with Louis.
Did she travel on the one-nighters with him?
Yeah, she travelled some with us. Not all the time, but a lot of times she travelled with us.
Yeah. She was quite a lady.
Yes.
Lil was.

That was really a -- that was really something. I'll tell you another thing. I had an experience -- you know, I was Louis' assistant, so Louis would play a number of dances, and Louis would go take a rest and I'd have to get up and take the band. Floor was just crowded. So I was up playing and directing the band, and after a while somebody just grabbed my hand. And I had my back turned to them, see, and they had my hand, holding it, you know. Floor was crowded. Then I noticed a look on the boys' -- the boys looked, I said, 'What's that (inaudible) got hold of my hand, and why are those guys looking so funny?' So when I turned around, this way, I turned around and there was this long-haired blond had hold of my hand. She had hold of my hand. And then -- I didn't object, I just come on and I kept my cool, you know. Of course, I was afraid if I'd jerk, it might jerk her down, see.
Yeah.
And I didn't want to do that, so I just kept my cool. And when they ended that number, she turned my hand loose and we just walked right on off the stand.
Yeah.
Of course, you had to be very careful down there with them people. They didn't -- at that time, they didn't understand.
I've read where Johnny Collins the manager's wife travelled with the band on that tour.
Yeah, that's right.
And that you got into Memphis, and some cops arrested the whole band because she was on the bus.

That's right. They certainly did. They arrested the whole band. And they came in and at the time, she was sitting in the seat, and Louis -- she was telling Louis something, Louis was on the edge of the arm of the bus, that's what it was, the arm of the seat, when the guys came in. And told the other -- (inaudible). When you stop to think of some of these things, you know, they are quite -- because some of the things that people that are sick-minded, you know, and still be ignorant. It's pain, but it's comical.
Told him, says -- told the captain, says, "You know what?" Oh, I forgot this recording, I forgot. He said, "He said this big, burly blankety-blankety-blank was sitting on
the arm of the seat that this white woman was sitting. So this guy said, "Why didn't you shoot him in the leg?"
Oh, really?
Isn't that something? Sure. That's what he said. "Why didn't you shoot him in the leg?"
God. That's unbelievable.

So -- yeah, so the only one that didn't get thrown in the clanker was Mike McKendrick. He was out somewhere, doing something and he didn't get a chance to get into that. And the whole thing was, the bus that Mrs. Collins had chartered was to take us from Jackson to Little Rock.

Well, they carried us from Jackson to Memphis, and then they wanted to change the bus. They wanted us to get into a different bus. Well, she said, "No, I want -- the bus that I want them to have --" so Louis could have this seat, to ra'r back in, to sleep. But they wanted to give us a little bus with the seats sitting straight up this way.
And that was the whole thing.
I see.
Yeah, they didn't want to do it, so this bus driver called the cops, and the cops said, Take them to the station.
Oh, the bus driver was the one that did it.
Yeah, so he said, "You know, every

trusty -- we had to have every trusty that he have in the clanker to come out, they had so much baggage, to get that baggage out." Because I had my piano accordion, I had the piano accordion, my Gladstone, my trumpet case, and then also my ordinary suitcase, see. And the carryall bag. See, we had carryall bags that we had shaving mugs and things in it.
Yeah.
And everybody had at least four or five -- you it'd take ten men --
That's a lot of baggage.
Was a lot of baggage.
Well, how did you get out?
The manager of the theatre where we had to come back to from Little Rock, we had to come back there and play after we played our engagement in Little Rock --
back to Memphis.
Memphis, he got them out. And then we caught the train, we had to catch a train, and we were late getting to Little Rock, but the crowd was still there. We got to Little Rock about 12:00.
Midnight?
Midnight, and they were still there, waiting on us.
Oh, to go back to New Orleans, speaking of dances, I read where there was a big dance for the
black people at an army base.

And the big dance -- the union there, the union and the officials, the political officials got together and they wouldn't let us have it. They wouldn't let them have the dance. And the people were just like that. I don't know why they said they wouldn't let us have it, but that's just what happened. I guess, near everybody in New Orleans was getting ready to go to that -- were ready for that dance. You really was right. They certainly didn't. Didn't let us have it. We really would have made the money that time. Really would have made money.
Well, how was the pay on that tour? The side men, how much did they make?
On the tour? On the --
That was at the depth of the Depression, I guess, '31.
Yeah, '31. Well, according to the way the scale and the salary was going, I think they did pretty good. I never did learn the other boys' salary, but my salary was a little more than their salary.
Because you did the arranging and was musical director (unintelligible)?
Because I was arranger and musical director. But I don't know just how that -- Louis was a very good fellow, too, because I know this one time, I -- all the

marbles wasn't up here, and I sent my wife some money. I just put the money in a letter and I just sent it to her. When she got it the letter was sealed up and the money was gone. So I told Louis about it, and borrowed some money from Louis so I could wire, so Louis let me have it.
Well, when I got paid off I went to give Louis back his money and he said, "Oh, no, no. You're doing more than that for me." And he didn't take it.
You say you had a piano accordion with you on the road. Did you use that -- you kept writing arrangements while you were travelling down in New Orleans?
Yes, I did, yeah. I kept writing arrangements.

Well, then, by the time you got back to Chicago, and the recording sessions with that band took place after you were on the road, what you recorded, was that what you'd been playing on the road, or did you write arrangements specifically for the recording dates? In '31?
Well, I think we recorded -- the only thing that we did, near as I can think now, the arrangements that I made, see, like 'High Society' --
That was a little later, Mr. Randolph.
Was it?
I'm talking about 'Chinatown', 'Stardust', 'You Can Depend On Me', 'Georgia on my Mind' --
Oh, 'Georgia on my Mind.'
"Lonesome Road," I Got Rhythm.
Yeah. Now, these was just -- it didn't take too much to do those backgrounds. Just whole four notes and -- there wasn't too much to do on those.
Well, had you done -- had the band been playing the arrangements?
Oh, yes, oh, yes. Yes, we had been playing them, before we had recorded them.
You had mentioned that sometimes you'd just take a stock and doctor it up a bit.
Doctor it up, that's right.
Was that pretty much what the band was playing at that time?
At -- well, --
Or had you written some complete arrangements of your own?
Well, sometimes I would do some complete things. Now, like, 'You Can Depend On Me,' you guess you heard -- (unintelligible) number. That was a complete arrangement.

I'm just looking at these song titles, and they have the date of their publication. And they were -- all except for 'Chinatown and Tiger Rag,' they were all published in '31, '32. So they were pop tunes.
Yeah, that's right.
This was the first recording of 'Stardust', I guess, wasn't it?
First recording -- I believe it was, first recording of 'Stardust'.
Or maybe Hoagy Carmichael had recorded it earlier.
I think we recorded 'Stardust' in Long Island.
Well, according to this, it was all done in Chicago, in November, I believe.

I think -- that's the time -- that was in Long Island, in this recording studio in Long Island. They probably got some of them mixed up, I might of said, in compiling them, the numbers together, because I remember that particular --
The band also did a recording for a Betty Boop cartoon, didn't it?
Yeah. That was Long Island.
That was in Long Island.
That was Long Island. A Betty Boop cartoon, and we did a short, 'Rhapsody in Black and Blue', with Sidney Easton.
Yeah. What were some of the tunes that you did for the Betty Boop cartoon and for the short?
Do you recall?
I believe "High Society" was on that. Because we had -- when we was said, ya ta ta, they had the spear shooting somebody, they had the spear going.
Oh, uh-huh.
Da ta ta, whee-oo, and that spear would go up, go out there.
You mentioned that when you joined the band in Detroit, and Louis made you musical director and said, it's your band.
Yes, uh-huh.
That the guys in the band didn't seem to like that. They resented that. Did that continue as time went by?
It continued until we got to New York. Now, that was just a syndicator of the band, a syndicator representing the band, like --
clique

-- and all of us did in there, and a certain element was there. But, now, you take -- like, Johnny Lindsay wasn't in the clique, Preston Jackson wasn't in it. See, he wasn't in it. Mr. Jackson was part of the instigator of me getting in there. He told Louis about me because -- Randolph here is asking what I'm talking about. He says that my arranging -- teaching his wife scoring, you know, and I guess
it became a kick for me, and Preston Jackson told him, and that rang a bell, you know.
(End of Side One, Tape 3.)
Well, the band broke up in New York. Is that correct? In '31.
Oh, the '31 band, yeah. Because Collins booked -- Collins had the band then. Connie's Inn
Collins.
Collins, Collins. And he booked Louis single overseas. I don't know whether he booked him in London or whether he booked him in Paris.
I think it was London, that time.
London, yes. And then we had to beat it back, when he came back here, back to Chicago.
To go back to the recording session, before you went off to New York. Do you remember what the recording fee was, what the scale was for recording?

Well, I -- to really tell you the truth, the recording fee -- I don't think we really got due justice on it, because Mike -- as I told you, I had charge of the arranging part of it, and directing the music -- I mean, the music director, and Mike had done most of the managing, like getting the uniforms and going between the men and the boss.
And the manager -- Louis says, "I know you told the --" McKendrick Louis told Mike McKinley, he say, "I know you boys are really
What does that mean?
It meant that we -- that you had plenty of money, that you made plenty of money.
Uh-huh.

See, so you made the Betty Boop cartoon, and you made the 'Rhapsody in Black and Blue,' then you had the recording session on top of that. And Mike told him, said, and all of that. Said, we only got -- I forgot how much that Mike told him that we got. Anyway, it wasn't enough to write home about. And, see, that was in the manager -- that was the manager's doings. The manager did that. He gypped me out of that money.
Johnny Collins has a pretty bad reputation. Was he a crook?
He must have been, because --
Or had connections with Capone and people like that?
I don't know. He must have been, because I remember, Joe Glaser said -- or, he says, 'I paid Collins the last that I owe him now.'
This was later, when he took over the band.
When he took over, yes. Because when Collins booked Louis over in London the last time I was with

the band, booked him over there, Louis said that he put Scotland Yard out looking for Collins. And they said Collins didn't even dock. He was on the boat with Louis, and when the time come, why, Louis was looking for him and he didn't even dock. He just went on back.

And then, when Louis came back and got the band together and everything like that, that's when Canetti Cossette came in there, I think, while Louis was going from London and going to France and all that, and booking himself and getting a manager. And then, when Louis came back and he started to work in Collins' -- he attached -- that's what you call it, attached the box office?
Yes.
Yeah. So Joe said -- I remember -- he said, "Well, we're free of Collins. I just paid Mr. Collins the last that we owe him."
It's funny how musicians get all messed up with people like that.
Yes, uh-huh.

Well, the -- how did you and Louis work together on the arrangements? You know, sometimes he's playing muted -- did you say, you should play muted here, or did he say, I'd like to play muted here, or just how did you work? Did he indicate the type of arrangement he wanted and the tempos and the keys and things like that?

No, no, he didn't. I worked freely. I worked freely, but in working freely, I knew his style, see, I knew his -- when I got in there I knew the man's style and I just arranged according to -- as I was making the arrangement I'd have him in mind and I just could hear what he would do at a certain thing, certain part, and I'd know how to spot him. And it was all right with him. And I'd just hand him his sheet.
Exactly what did you write for -- what did his part consist of? Last week you said that -- we were talking about "High Society," that you had written the ending for him.

Yes. Well, his part would be -- like, if I do an ensemble, he'd take the lead. I'd give him the lead and I'd be taking the second part. But I'd always arrange to -- make the arrangement so that he would have ample time to give -- to relax his armature before he would have to come in and work, because he would work so hard, you know. So I never did write in a way so that it would jam him in any way.
This was during a period where he's supposed to -- he would announce that we're going to do "Tiger Rag" and I'll hit 100 high C's for the musicians in the audience?
Now, that's -- now, he worked freely with that. And all I would have to do is just look out for the horns, just see that the horns -- that, if you and I were
playing saxophone, say, that if we start -- that you and I don't make the same tone, you know.
Uh-huh.
You know how that -- so I didn't consider those things. But his arrangements -- go ahead, let it go.

Uh-huh. Well, in your arranging, you don't seem to have been influenced by any of the arrangers that most of us know about, like Ellington or Fletcher Henderson, Don Redman. Who was your influence? Did you ever hear any of the arrangements that Bill Challis made?
That who?
Bill Challis.
Bill Challis.
He arranged for the Whitman band and Goldkette's Gene Coyat's band and --

Bill -- as a matter of fact, I don't think I know the name, but I heard those bands. They played some very good arrangements. But, now, for instance, say if you had a band and you wanted me to make an arrangement -- let's just say, if you wanted me to make -- say, I want you to make me a knockout arrangement on 'Poor Butterfly'.
Well, what I would do, I'd say, you want me to make a knockout arrangement on 'Poor Butterfly'. I would try to see if I could hear two or three arrangements on 'Poor Butterfly'.
Now, when I hear those arrangements, not to extract anything, but to get away from them.
To see what had been done.

Who's that?
Was Muggsy Spanier.
Well, Bobby Hackett --
Yeah, Bobby Hackett was another one.
Bobby just loved Louis.
Louis, yes.
And everybody said he sounded like Bix.
Yeah.

But I've worked some gigs with him and he played Muskrat Ramble. He played what Louis played on the Hot Five record, in 1925, '36, whenever it was. But he played it with Bobby Hackett's tone. And I was playing one time and (unintelligible), I said Goddamn, he's playing Louis' thing. And we talked about it afterwards, and he loved Louis. Oh, he loved Louis. Well, we all did.
Yes.
Great musician. Well, --

And that gravel voice Louis got. But you know, I can imitate Louis so -- and the way he blows his trumpet, his singing and his talking. Well, I should, I was with the man right up on five years and I idolized the man.
Yeah?
Yeah.
You all were very close.
It was Jesus first, and I guess it was a tossup between Louis and my wife. Because I know Louis was right in there.
I think that's a good note to end on.

Yes, sir. That's my influence. I put God first and then after that, then I have to take all the rest of them. You know, one time I had a mind to doing an act like this, when I would go out there and started singing and I'd sing a part of it and I'd tell Louis to come in and you do your part, Louis. Then I'd sing like Louis, and I'd -- I would say, hey, now, look out, Randy, now you take this one. Then I would start to singing, you know, one of those things. Well, I don't know. I get to thinking, well, here I'm here, teaching. I better just stay on here, teaching, instead of getting out here on the road. And I'd get my sleep now, where I can get my rest. Got in the senior years, I'm 78. So it would be best to cool it, don't you think?
I guess so. I know Eubie
Blake's still going. Eubie's 93 now, I think.
Yeah, he's still going, eh?
Amazing.

Well, I don't know. I get to thinking, I just want to put some talent out there now, try to see if I can get some people doing some things. Get them to do things that I want them to do. Try to get them to do the things I want them to do. And I want to get this opera going, if I can.

I'm going to try to keep in touch with you because I want to keep you informed about this opera, because I want to -- you probably can help me to get a sponsor or an agent or something. If you find out what the opera is going to be like.
After the interview, Mr. Randolph asked me to correct birth date, as listed in Chilton's Who's Who in Jazz. It is listed as July 28, 1899. He says the correct date is January 28, 1899.
(End of proceedings.)

segments.title: Copyright notice and opening of the 1977 Smithsonian interview
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright notices, the Smithsonian title page (Tapes One and Two, Chicago, February 13, 1977) and Don DeMichael's spoken introduction.

segments.title: Birth in 1899 and how he got the name Zilner
segments.summary: Randolph gives his birth date and place and explains that a German repairman told his seamstress mother to name a baby boy Zilner.

segments.title: Learning guitar from a friend named Lawrence, and playing Jim Canen
segments.summary: At about ten he learned finger-style guitar and the blues from Lawrence, and plays a demonstration of Jim Canen with a modern ending.

segments.title: Beer-drinking parties, buck dancing and shows with his brother in Arkansas
segments.summary: He and his brother played guitar and sang for local parties for fun, then put on shows with paid admission in Jennings and Chico.

segments.title: Presbyterian school at Hot Springs and his brother joining the circus
segments.summary: Their mother sent the boys to a parochial school in Hot Springs in 1912; his brother ran off to Ringling Brothers, performing a side-show act with Mantan Moreland.

segments.title: Piano lessons and church recitals at the school
segments.summary: He studied piano from the assistant principal using Matthews' graded course, and played the King Alcohol role in a school play.

segments.title: Ragtime and Blind Boone: what he knew of St. Louis-area piano
segments.summary: DeMichael asks about ragtime repertoire and Blind Boone's piano rolls; Randolph knew Boone only from his mother's talk.

segments.title: Copying James P. Johnson piano rolls
segments.summary: Randolph copied James P. Johnson's Carolina Shout from rolls but could not stretch the left-hand tenths.

segments.title: Deciding to be a musician and his father's objection to guitar players
segments.summary: His father refused him a guitar because guitarists were pimps and rounders with gold teeth; Randolph says he might have become a guitarist like Joe Pass.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Buying a trumpet and playing in a band in Helena, then Biddle University
segments.summary: With no piano at home he bought a trumpet, played in a Helena town band around 1916 and entered Biddle University in 1917.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: March repertoire and first hearing ragtime, hokum and jazz records
segments.summary: The Arkansas band played marches and patriotic songs; he knew Sweatman's records and ragtime turning into jazz, and his solid legit trumpet solos.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: A local pianist who embellished popular songs
segments.summary: Randolph recalls a pianist (Benton Overstreet, he thinks) who improvised ornaments on popular songs.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: The Biddle marching band under T. B. Jones
segments.summary: At Biddle he played in a 25-30 piece marching band; his improvised turn-back lines annoyed director T. B. Jones.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Playing Coleridge-Taylor's Hiawatha's Wedding Feast at Biddle
segments.summary: First-chair trumpet on Coleridge-Taylor's piece with a violinist and a tenor soloist; he also notes the school became Johnson C. Smith.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Playing from the porch of a Charlotte theater for Hawaiian films
segments.summary: The college band played Isle of My Golden Dreams and similar numbers above a theater for the movies and earned a little money.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: The nickname Jazz Baby and the few records he heard
segments.summary: Schoolmates called him Jazz Baby although he had not studied arranging; he heard few records because there was no record player.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Summer at Page's Park in Durham: dance band, and marriage in 1919
segments.summary: After Biddle he played a summer dance band in Durham that mixed ragtime, popular waltzes and few blues; he met and married his wife there in 1919, and he dislikes today's popular music.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Leading the band in a Pigmeat Markham show
segments.summary: He led the band for a small touring show starring Pigmeat Markham around the South until it disbanded back in Durham.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Sullivan's five-piece dixieland band at a Danville dance school
segments.summary: He joined drummer Sullivan's faking band of drums, piano, clarinet, trombone and trumpet; the dance school paid well until the owner vanished in the last week.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Hippodrome Theater in Danville: Walter Morrow's trio and TOBA shows
segments.summary: He played sideman in a three-piece theater band for touring shows, using arrangements by Eddie Heywood Sr. and backing TOBA acts like the Whitman Sisters.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Theater pay and being laid off when business turned slow
segments.summary: He earned $25 a week while the manager kept sending the band home on slow days, then laid off the trumpet; Randolph says it taught him to root for the house.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Playing in a medicine show band
segments.summary: A four-piece band played fast marches while a doctor sold a dollar-a-bottle tonic, staying three to four weeks in each town.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Escape artist, comedians and the medicine show's break-up in Cincinnati
segments.summary: He describes the show's acts, including an escape artist who expanded his chest against the ropes, and how the show broke up after Greensboro and Cincinnati.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Playing the minstrel show with J. L. Cronan's carnival
segments.summary: The trombonist wired a 42-car carnival, and Randolph played ballyhoo in town to draw crowds, nearly laughing at the barker's closing line.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Taking over the band at Watkins's theater in Durham
segments.summary: He returned to Durham to lead the band at a theater owned by Watkins for three or four months before going home to Arkansas.

segments.chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
segments.title: Drugstore band in Helena with Joseph Patterson and the Syncopated Six
segments.summary: He played in the back of a crowded Helena drugstore, brought in guitarist Joseph Patterson, and the owner added the Syncopated Six, including Floyd Campbell and Cranston Hamilton.

segments.title: Arriving in St. Louis and meeting Charlie Creath, his sister and Zutty Singleton
segments.summary: Randolph moved to St. Louis with Patterson, was introduced to Charlie Creath, was given a job by Creath's sister Marge, and met Zutty Singleton there.

segments.title: Playing silent pictures at the Criterion Theater from cue sheets
segments.summary: Taking over Shirley Clay's theater job, he read overtures and Sam Fox folio music matched to film cue sheets.

segments.title: Starting harmony and thorough bass lessons with Eddie Hudson
segments.summary: With free daytime hours, he found a teacher and studied harmony and thorough bass with Eddie Hudson from 1922 to 1925, leaving St. Louis around 1926.

segments.title: White bands in St. Louis: Trumbauer, Beiderbecke and the Arcadia
segments.summary: Asked about white musicians, he only heard some of their tunes and knew of the Arcadia Ballroom.

segments.title: Four years of lessons with Eddie Hudson and what he taught
segments.summary: Randolph studied Goodrich's Analysis of Music with Hudson, passed this on to his pupils, and recalls Hudson's advice about not forming habits you cannot do without.

segments.title: A jealous theater leader and the move to the Chauffeur's Club
segments.summary: The theater leader Cranshaw resented his piano and demanded he buy a new horn, so Randolph took Shirley Clay's higher-paying job at the Chauffeur's Club.

segments.title: The Chauffeur's Club dixieland band and playing Snag It
segments.summary: He played in Pat Powell's dixieland band with Isaac Jefferson and others, and answered Powell's punishing Snag It tempo with triple-tongued trumpet.

segments.title: Waitresses, river-boat bands and Eddie Inge's offer of a Milwaukee job
segments.summary: Waitresses wondered why the trumpeter never came upstairs; Eddie Inge, who had been watching him, phoned from Milwaukee with a Roof Garden job.

segments.title: Hearing Louis Armstrong's records and arranging his tunes
segments.summary: He had no night off to hear the river-boat bands, but knew Armstrong's Hot Five records and Snag It, made arrangements of Armstrong tunes, and was moved by the Bessie Smith St. Louis Blues record.

segments.title: Hearing every tune in two veins, Armstrong's and Coleman Hawkins's
segments.summary: Randolph says he hears tunes in both a Louis vein and a Hawkins vein and teaches this idiom to pupils.

segments.title: The Wisconsin Roof Garden and the Bernie Young band in Milwaukee
segments.summary: A white-clientele ballroom atop the Wisconsin Theater, Peacock's Alley, with a white band and Bernie Young's band billed as Creoles.

segments.title: His arranging style: counterpoint, offbeat voicings and chord colors
segments.summary: Randolph describes writing in counterpoint rather than concerted style and finding his ahead-of-time harmonies hard to put over.

segments.title: Instrumentation and swing of the Bernie Young band
segments.summary: A twelve-piece unit with three brass, three reeds and four rhythm, the same as Armstrong's 1931 band, which he says swung.

segments.title: Bernie Young band sidemen: Cassino Simpson, Quinn Wilson, McKendrick, Jackson
segments.summary: Randolph names the pianists, bassists and others who passed through Young's band and talks about meeting McKendrick and Preston Jackson there.

segments.title: Bernie Young's role as business-minded second trumpet, and the move to Chicago
segments.summary: Young played second trumpet and handled business while Randolph led the section; after about three years at the Roof Garden the whole band moved to Chicago in 1929.

segments.title: House band at Chicago's Savoy Ballroom and a failed Tulsa booking
segments.summary: Bernie Young's band was Savoy house band for about a year until Music Corporation of America booked it to Tulsa for a contract that fell through.

segments.title: Arranging for Earl Hines and teaching Lil Armstrong to score
segments.summary: Back in Chicago he began arranging and gigging, wrote for Earl Hines's Grand Terrace band and taught scoring to Lil Hardin at his home studio.

segments.title: Union trouble as a transfer member from Milwaukee
segments.summary: The Chicago local blocked him from a Regal Theater job as a transfer member, but could not remove him from Louis Armstrong's band because Armstrong insisted.

segments.title: Joining Armstrong in Detroit in 1931 and who assembled the band
segments.summary: Randolph joined at the Greystone Ballroom in June 1931 and, asked whether he selected the men, names George James, Al Washington, Tubby Hall, Johnny Lindsay and Preston Jackson.

segments.title: Armstrong tells him on opening night: this is your band
segments.summary: On the Greystone opening night Armstrong made Randolph take the band, embarrassing him when he stomped off seated, and he then directed sets whenever Armstrong rested.

segments.title: Bandsmen's resentment and the huddles that scattered when he approached
segments.summary: Randolph felt resented by some of the men, though not only New Orleans musicians, who would break up their huddles when he walked over.

segments.title: Armstrong's path from 1929 to the April 1931 band, and who joined when
segments.summary: DeMichael reviews Armstrong's years with Dickerson, New York and Les Hite and his 1931 arrest; Randolph and Lindsay were added to an existing band, and he was not in the band for the Showboat trouble.

segments.title: Meeting Armstrong and proving he could read music
segments.summary: Randolph took a tune to Armstrong at the Regal, and Armstrong sang the difficult intervals at sight, convincing Randolph that the rumor he could not read was false.

segments.title: Writing the 1931 book: stock inserts and the choir on Wrap Your Troubles in Dreams
segments.summary: He supplied some arrangements and inserts into stocks; the band's choir singing was done ad hoc and he felt it sounded poor with no backing from Armstrong.

segments.title: Musical director, with McKendrick as business manager
segments.summary: Randolph rehearsed the band and directed the shows while Mike McKendrick handled uniforms, travel and business; endings behind Armstrong were felt rather than written.

segments.title: Why he never arranged When the Saints Go Marching In
segments.summary: Armstrong asked for a Saints arrangement, but Randolph avoided it as a religious song until he heard it from a sound truck after he had left.

segments.title: Armstrong's repertoire beyond the recorded pop tunes
segments.summary: Besides pop and show tunes, the band played older numbers like Shine and Black and Blue, which Armstrong had recorded before coming back to Chicago.

segments.title: Adding endings and introductions; the Stardust motif Basie reused
segments.summary: He doctored stocks with intros and endings and developed a motif on Stardust that Randolph says Count Basie later turned into One O'Clock Jump.

segments.title: Writing the High Society arrangement and Armstrong's ending
segments.summary: Randolph wrote the arrangement, using the New Orleans clarinet chorus for saxophones and chords mirrored above the harmony, and also wrote Armstrong's ending.

segments.title: The Guy Lombardo saxophone sound and vibrato versus tremolo
segments.summary: Armstrong liked a Lombardo-like sax vibrato; Randolph voiced differently and explains moderation and steady vibrato versus tremolo.

segments.title: Other trumpeters said his tone was bad: Preston Jackson and the Spivak comparison
segments.summary: When he arrived from Milwaukee, trumpeters knocked his tone; Preston Jackson heard him play and found nothing wrong, and Randolph says he played like Charlie Spivak.

segments.title: The human voice as the greatest instrument
segments.summary: Randolph argues instruments should play as one sings and that the voice is God's instrument, which is why singers earn more.

segments.title: Armstrong's singing, his playing and what it was like working with him
segments.summary: Armstrong played the way he sang; playing with him every night was a ball, and he was a down-home man, not a distant leader.

segments.title: Letting Armstrong sleep rather than make a Washington broadcast
segments.summary: On a one-nighter run in Washington Randolph refused to wake Armstrong for a broadcast, angering Joe Glaser and Armstrong's wife Alpha.

segments.chapter: Sunset Cafe, Pass in Review and rebuilding the band
segments.title: Opening of part two, February 20, 1977
segments.summary: Title page and heading for the second session, tapes 3, 4 and 5.

segments.chapter: Sunset Cafe, Pass in Review and rebuilding the band
segments.title: The Sunset All Stars under Cal Dickerson and Randolph's Peanut Vendor audition
segments.summary: Glaser hired Cal Dickerson to put together the Sunset band; Armstrong had insisted on Randolph, who won Glaser over by playing and singing The Peanut Vendor in Armstrong's manner.

segments.chapter: Sunset Cafe, Pass in Review and rebuilding the band
segments.title: Jabbo Smith, Leon Scott and rival-to-Armstrong rumors
segments.summary: Jabbo Smith stayed in the Sunset band a short time, replaced by Leon Scott; Randolph is unsure about attempts to build Jabbo as an Armstrong rival.

segments.chapter: Sunset Cafe, Pass in Review and rebuilding the band
segments.title: Touring with the Pass in Review unit of the 1933 World's Fair show
segments.summary: Glaser sent Randolph and Sunset men to join Leo Salkins's Pass in Review revue, which toured Iowa and the state with sixty white performers.

segments.chapter: Sunset Cafe, Pass in Review and rebuilding the band
segments.title: Segregation ends the Pass in Review tour and Armstrong calls
segments.summary: Because Black and white performers could not share a stage in the South, the show dumped them; then Armstrong, courted by both Mezzrow and Glaser as manager, contacted Randolph.

segments.chapter: Sunset Cafe, Pass in Review and rebuilding the band
segments.title: Organizing the second band for Armstrong; Canetti and the copied scores
segments.summary: After Armstrong's return from Europe Randolph put a band together; the booker Canetti held Armstrong's music, so Bobby Wall copied Randolph's scores and Glaser hocked the Sunset for uniforms.

segments.title: Personnel of the first 1931 band
segments.summary: DeMichael and Randolph list the men: Tubby Hall, Lester Boone, Charlie Alexander, Al Washington, George James and Mike McKendrick, and that he joined at the Greystone.

segments.title: Armstrong's welcome in New Orleans and hearing Louis Prima
segments.summary: A Black crowd lifted Armstrong on arrival and the band stayed at Patterson's Hotel; Randolph heard a band singing in Armstrong's manner and it was Louis Prima.

segments.title: Four months at the Suburban Gardens supper club
segments.summary: A ballroom, supper club and gambling place with only the band featured; booked for four weeks, the band stayed four months and Armstrong was popular with the white crowd.

segments.title: The Pelicans broadcast and Armstrong's Grant took Richmond line
segments.summary: Armstrong, an honorary member of the Pelicans baseball team, said on air they would take the other team like Grant took Richmond and letters poured in.

segments.title: Armstrong's habits on the road and the Louis and Lil stage act
segments.summary: Armstrong did not jam after work but went to bed; Randolph praises the immaculate comic act of Louis and Lil in a New Orleans theater.

segments.title: A woman grabbing his hand while he led the band
segments.summary: While leading with his back to the floor, a blond white woman took hold of his hand and he kept his cool until the number ended.

segments.title: Arrest of the whole band in Memphis over a bus and Mrs. Collins
segments.summary: Police arrested the band after a dispute over the chartered bus and Johnny Collins's wife, an officer asked why they had not shot Armstrong in the leg, and bags took ten men to unload.

segments.title: A big New Orleans dance blocked by the union and officials
segments.summary: A dance for Black patrons at an army base was blocked by union and political officials after the whole city was ready to attend.

segments.title: Pay on the 1931 tour and Armstrong lending him money
segments.summary: Randolph earned somewhat more than the others as arranger and director, and Armstrong lent him money for his wife and refused repayment.

segments.title: Arrangements for the 1931 recordings: Stardust, Chinatown, Georgia on My Mind
segments.summary: He wrote on the road with a piano accordion; the recorded titles were pop tunes of 1931-32 the band had already played, though he places the Stardust recording in Long Island.

segments.title: The Betty Boop cartoon and the short Rhapsody in Black and Blue
segments.summary: The band recorded a Betty Boop cartoon and a short with Sidney Easton in Long Island, including High Society and a spear-throwing scene.

segments.title: The clique against him, and the band breaking up in New York
segments.summary: Resentment lasted until New York, though Lindsay and Preston Jackson stayed outside the clique; Collins then booked Armstrong alone abroad and the band returned to Chicago.

segments.title: Recording fees and the manager Johnny Collins
segments.summary: Randolph thinks the band was shortchanged on the cartoon, short and records by Collins, whom he and DeMichael suspect was a crook; Glaser later paid off Collins.

segments.title: Arranging for Armstrong: writing to his style without instructions
segments.summary: Randolph wrote freely with Armstrong's style in mind, gave him the lead, and left him time to rest his lip.

segments.title: Avoiding other arrangers' ideas and praying for his own
segments.summary: Asked about influences like Challis, Ellington and Redman, he says he listens to other arrangements only to get away from them and prays for his ideas.

segments.title: Bandleaders watering down his difficult arrangements
segments.summary: Bandleaders such as Highland told him they had to cut his arrangements because commercial bands lacked time to perfect them; Swinging Cats was only played passably.

segments.title: Benny Goodman's reaction to the Swing Man arrangement, and his planned opera
segments.summary: Goodman called Old Man River too simple a tune for such an arrangement but played Swing Man; Randolph says he is working on an opera with choreography.

segments.title: Comparing the 1931, 1933 and 1934 Armstrong bands
segments.summary: The 1931 band was almost a combo of about ten, the 1933 band was cleaner, and DeMichael thinks the 1934 band had the most interesting arrangements.

segments.title: Teddy Wilson, Yank Porter and the Oldham brothers in the 1933 band
segments.summary: Randolph hired Teddy Wilson from Chicago, along with Yank Porter, the Johnson brothers and the Oldham brothers.

segments.title: Arranging for Earl Hines, Erskine Tate and others after 1931
segments.summary: Between the bands he arranged and gigged, with Earl Hines as a main customer and also Erskine Tate, Clyde Snyder and stage-show acts at the Regal.

segments.title: Don't hire Randolph, he will run your band
segments.summary: On an excursion boat, a leader got sore when Randolph played Tiger Rag at his own tempo, and word spread that Randolph runs the band.

segments.title: Picking the musicians for the 1933 band
segments.summary: Randolph chose the Oldham boys and Mike McKendrick sent in trumpeter Stump Whitlock, after Armstrong wired both of them.

segments.title: Directing the Four Blazers' act at the Pearl Theater in Philadelphia
segments.summary: The 1931 band played the week Ellington was off; Randolph worked out the tempos for the Four Blazers but misjudged the tempo at the performance.

segments.title: The January 1933 Victor sessions and how the music was assembled
segments.summary: DeMichael lists the many titles recorded days after Armstrong's return; Randolph says some were head-arranged in the studio and he had prepared Swing You Cats and High Society.

segments.title: High Society and the mirroring of chords
segments.summary: Randolph denies Luis Russell wrote High Society and explains his chord mirroring with a pivotal chord, later found in Miller's New Harmonic Devices, which New York loved.

segments.title: The 1933 band's choir singing and the viper's language of Sweet Sue
segments.summary: Randolph had the band singing like Fred Waring's Pennsylvanians; Sweet Sue was Budd Johnson's idea, with Armstrong interpreting viper talk.

segments.title: Armstrong selected the tunes and put them on the wax
segments.summary: Armstrong mostly chose the songs at the first session and liked to say they would put them on the wax.

segments.title: Song choices and Sleepytime Down South as theme
segments.summary: Randolph says Armstrong simply liked the Southern-flavored songs, not a managed image, recalls the press reaction to his Yes, Lord and notes Sleepytime as his theme.

segments.title: The pianists: Teddy Wilson, Charlie Beal, Sid Catlett session and Harry Dial
segments.summary: Wilson and Yank Porter went on the road, a California pianist replaced Wilson, and Sid Catlett only made a record session.

segments.title: Writing Don't Play Me Cheap with Harry Dial
segments.summary: Randolph and Harry Dial wrote Don't Play Me Cheap, taking the title from a Chicago phrase about South Center department store.

segments.title: I Wonder Who, the Laughin' Louie record and loose studio sessions
segments.summary: They try to identify a tune from Laughin' Louie and discuss the humor and relaxed atmosphere of the sessions with Armstrong keeping everyone laughing.

segments.title: Budd and Keg Johnson as soloists
segments.summary: The 1933 band had more sideman solos; Randolph praises Budd Johnson on tenor and Keg Johnson's lip-trilling trombone.

segments.title: Rehearsing at the Appomattox Club and who really hired the Johnsons
segments.summary: Randolph found the Johnson brothers, rehearsed the band, and says Jack Oglesby copied record parts, disputing Budd's claim that Armstrong sent for them.

segments.title: Why banjo and tuba came back in the 1933 band
segments.summary: Asked why the rhythm section returned to banjo and tuba, Randolph thinks it was McKendrick's idea.

segments.title: Trumpet solos on records and Armstrong featuring Whitlock in Louisville
segments.summary: Armstrong rarely featured other trumpeters on records, but at dances he featured Stump Whitlock, especially in Whitlock's hometown of Louisville.

segments.title: Staying back on You Can Depend On Me and Armstrong's Lionel Hampton record
segments.summary: Randolph played the background trumpet softly because Armstrong, remembering how he had held down Lionel Hampton on a Les Hite record, wanted him to stay back.

segments.title: The 1933 book, and Armstrong is the whole band
segments.summary: The book mixed arrangements, heads and stocks; Armstrong told him not to be bothered by people saying he was the whole band, and they talked music and the Saints.

segments.title: Armstrong's mouthpiece, copied by Charlie Allen
segments.summary: Randolph used Armstrong's spare mouthpiece, had Charlie Allen copy it when Armstrong asked for it back, and shows its round cushion.

segments.title: How Armstrong could play so high
segments.summary: Randolph tried to copy Armstrong's open-mouth high-note embouchure in a mirror and cannot understand how air did not escape.

segments.title: Giving Armstrong lessons to rebuild his chops in 1934
segments.summary: After France Armstrong's lip was sore and he lost his callus; Randolph gave him exercises, to the amazement of drummer Gable.

segments.title: Collins sends the 1933 band home and Armstrong recontacts him
segments.summary: Collins booked Armstrong in France and sent the band to Chicago; on returning, Armstrong contacted Randolph and McKendrick.

segments.title: Personnel of the third band, the 1934 band that never recorded
segments.summary: Randolph struggles to recall the sidemen: Barnett, the Oldhams, Leon Washington, Dunlap, Milton Fletcher, Prentice McCarey, and a guitarist who doubled bassoon.

segments.title: Sung vocal arrangements in the 1934 band
segments.summary: The 1934 band sang I'm Just an Ordinary Human and the background to Kings Don't Mean a Thing in deep harmony like a glee club.

segments.title: The original Old Man Mose and the publishers' revamped version
segments.summary: Randolph says his Old Man Mose verse began on the fifth in minor and the publishers rewrote it on the tonic; he notes he often had to go along with the program.

segments.title: Kings Don't Mean a Thing: the sung dominant chord and Armstrong's obbligato
segments.summary: The whole band sang a big raised-fifth chord and Armstrong riffed between phrases, but Chicago never heard the arrangement.

segments.title: Taking the 1934 band East, who would direct, and its size
segments.summary: The band went East towards the Howard Theater with questions about who would direct the shows; it had five brass, four saxes and a rhythm section.

segments.title: Glaser replaces the band with Luis Russell's New York band
segments.summary: At the Great White Way (formerly Connie's Inn) the union demanded standby men, so Glaser dropped Randolph's band and used Luis Russell's local New York band.

segments.title: The bassoon in his arrangements, and comedians burlesquing it
segments.summary: A guitarist doubled bassoon and Randolph used it extensively; he resents radio comedy turning a beautiful instrument into a clown.

segments.title: Did Armstrong's chops ever come back after 1934?
segments.summary: DeMichael hears less brilliance in the 1935 Russell records; Randolph saw Armstrong still picking at his lip with a mirror and agrees.

segments.title: Armstrong's work pace, and the band that would not back him up
segments.summary: Randolph says the men did not support him; leaving New Orleans for Little Rock in 1934 he went door to door rousting late sidemen.

segments.title: Armstrong gives Glaser the reins; the union deal and end of the band
segments.summary: After the lateness Armstrong told Glaser he had full say over the band, and then the union arrangement brought Luis Russell in and let go the whole band.

segments.title: Writing to Roosevelt and becoming a WPA conductor
segments.summary: Randolph wrote to the President, got an answer from Steve Early, and was assigned an A-1 conductor on the WPA music project.

segments.title: Building the WPA band from relief rolls
segments.summary: He began playing trumpet to fill the unit, recruited men from relief and then had the cream of the crop.

segments.title: WPA band members: Quinn Wilson, Henderson Smith and Yardbird Williams
segments.summary: He recalls Punch Miller possibly, Quinn Wilson, Henderson Smith and trombonist Walter Yardbird Williams.

segments.title: A swinging dance-band William Tell, played for Hal Kemp
segments.summary: The WPA dance band played Randolph's swing arrangement of William Tell, which Hal Kemp came to hear at noon.

segments.title: Playing schools and a Jewish old folks' home: the trombonist who changed the program
segments.summary: The band played free at schools and homes; a trombonist always swapped his announced number, once breaking down while playing his mother's favorite hymn.

segments.title: Work schedule and monthly pay on the WPA project
segments.summary: Musicians played nights or rehearsed 9 to 1, and received a regular monthly income.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: The WPA band is cut and Woody Herman sends a telegram
segments.summary: The project cut the jazz band while keeping the long-hair musicians, and the next night Woody Herman wired him to join; he stayed to about 1940.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: Arranging for Woody Herman's band
segments.summary: He travelled with the band, rehearsed his own charts including Peace Brother and Pick-a-Rib, and wrote the jazz numbers while others did sweet tunes.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: A William Tell arrangement for Duke Ellington
segments.summary: He wrote a special William Tell for Duke Ellington, who said he would play it, but Ben Webster told him it never got done.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: Hearing arrangements in his head: why his charts were called hard
segments.summary: He denies writing hard music for its own sake, describes hearing a whole band in his head, and says his eyesight now limits his arranging.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: Leaving Woody Herman and passing on a chance to join Duke
segments.summary: He was with Herman about two years, and told Ellington he could not play trumpet after so long.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: Arranging for Fletcher Henderson, in his own style
segments.summary: Henderson, busy writing for Benny Goodman, hired Randolph to arrange for his band, the Grand Terrace band with Roy Eldridge and Chu Berry.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: A walk-in composer and the China Boy arrangement for Henderson
segments.summary: A young songwriter had Randolph score a big-band arrangement that Henderson played, and Henderson then asked for three China arrangements, of which Randolph did China Boy.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: Leading the small stage band at the Indiana Theater in 1941
segments.summary: He took the band onstage at the theater at 43rd and Indiana after the singer Lamille, with saxophone, drums and piano, sometimes himself playing both trumpet and piano.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: Recording piano with his kids, Two Honeys in a Comb
segments.summary: He recorded with his young trio, whose trumpeter Lucius scatted and played harmonized lines, until the Army took him.

segments.chapter: Woody Herman, Henderson and the Indiana Theater
segments.title: Playing head arrangements for touring acts at the Indiana
segments.summary: The theater band backed acts from the Oriental Theater and Chez Paree, reading music only sometimes and otherwise following a sung melody.

segments.title: Writing for Armstrong after 1935: Cavalier Rusty Cannon and the Old Man Mose record
segments.summary: He wrote Armstrong an arrangement but regretted writing the piano solo; the Armstrong-Russell Old Man Mose record played just one note.

segments.title: Respecting what a composer wrote, and why he dislikes rock and roll
segments.summary: Randolph objects to others reshaping a composer's number and says he is just one man in disliking rock and roll for its structure.

segments.title: Structure versus improvisation in early jazz
segments.summary: Early New Orleans bands had wonderful ideas but lacked development; improvising is like a bubble that bursts, while writing records the idea.

segments.title: Armstrong as supreme improviser, I Can't Give You Anything But Love
segments.summary: Both agree Armstrong was the greatest melodic improviser with form; Randolph points to his I Can't Give You Anything But Love as an eye-opener.

segments.title: Bunny Berigan playing Stardust and Armstrong's All-American pick
segments.summary: Randolph mistook Bunny Berigan for Armstrong; Armstrong told him he picked Berigan as his favorite trumpeter because he played Armstrong's style.

segments.title: Muggsy Spanier and Bobby Hackett playing like Armstrong
segments.summary: They name Spanier and Hackett as Armstrong disciples; DeMichael recalls Hackett playing Armstrong's Muskrat Ramble solo.

segments.title: Idolizing Armstrong after five years with him
segments.summary: Randolph can imitate Armstrong's voice and horn, was with him nearly five years and ranks him just behind God and his wife.

segments.title: Teaching in his senior years and hopes for an opera
segments.summary: At 78 he prefers to stay teaching rather than tour, comments on Eubie Blake, and asks DeMichael to help find a sponsor for his opera.

segments.title: Correction of Randolph's birth date and end of proceedings
segments.summary: DeMichael's note that Randolph asked to correct Chilton's listing to January 28, 1899.
